lead: This unit explains how raw bits become signals that travel over wires, fiber or air. After finishing, the student can choose the right media and coding for a given speed and distance and estimate the maximum data rate.
about: Unit 2 covers the physical layer in eight short chapters. 2.1 explains analog and digital signals and how they are sampled and quantised. 2.2 describes attenuation, distortion and noise that degrade signals. 2.3 derives the Nyquist and Shannon limits on data rate. 2.4 lists guided (copper, fibre) and unguided (radio, satellite) media. 2.5 shows line‑coding schemes for digital links. 2.6 introduces analog transmission and digital modulation methods. 2.7 compares FDM, TDM and WDM multiplexing. 2.8 (advanced) gives a brief view of spread‑spectrum techniques. Each chapter builds on the previous one, moving from signal basics to media choice, coding, modulation and sharing.

chapters.idea: Convert analog waveforms to digital bit streams and back.
chapters.depth: Define analog (continuous‑time) and digital (discrete‑time) signals. Explain sampling, Nyquist rate, quantisation and PCM. Mention other names such as continuous‑time signal, discrete‑time signal and pulse‑code modulation. Only a few universities teach this in depth.

figure.aria: Shows the steps from an analog sinusoid to a digital bit stream.

chapters.example: A 1 kHz sinusoid is sampled at 8 kHz and quantised with 8 bits. How many bits are transmitted per second?
chapters.trap: Using a sampling rate lower than twice the highest frequency.
chapters.leave: Circuit details of ADC/DAC are covered in lab sessions.

chapters.idea: Signals lose strength and quality while traveling through a medium.
chapters.depth: Explain attenuation (dB/km), distortion (band‑limiting), and noise (thermal, shot). Define signal‑to‑noise ratio (SNR). Other names: loss, inter‑symbol interference. Only a few universities teach this in depth.

figure.aria: Shows a signal passing through attenuation and noise before reaching the receiver.

chapters.example: A 1 V peak signal travels through a cable with 2 dB attenuation and encounters a noise floor of –90 dBm. Compute the received SNR in dB.
chapters.trap: Mixing linear ratios with dB values without conversion.
chapters.leave: Equalisation techniques are discussed in Chapter 5.

chapters.idea: Maximum achievable data rate is limited by bandwidth and SNR.
chapters.depth: State Nyquist formula C = 2B·log₂M for noiseless channels and Shannon formula C = B·log₂(1+SNR) for noisy channels. Define bandwidth B, signal levels M, and SNR. Also known as channel capacity.

figure.aria: Shows how capacity grows with SNR according to the Shannon formula.

chapters.example: A channel has 3 MHz bandwidth and an SNR of 30 dB. What is the theoretical maximum data rate?
chapters.trap: Putting the SNR value in dB directly into the log₂ term.
chapters.leave: Practical coding overhead is covered in later chapters.

chapters.idea: Media are divided into guided (wired) and unguided (wireless) types.
chapters.depth: Describe twisted‑pair, coaxial cable, single‑mode and multimode fibre (guided) and radio, microwave, satellite, infrared (unguided). Mention typical bandwidths and attenuation. Also called wired vs wireless media.

figure.aria: Lists common guided and unguided transmission media.

chapters.example: Compare the maximum data rate of a 100 m Cat5e link (1 Gbps) with a 10 km single‑mode fibre link (10 Gbps).
chapters.trap: Assuming all media have the same attenuation per kilometre.
chapters.leave: Fiber mode details are given in Chapter 6.

chapters.idea: Map binary bits to voltage or current levels for transmission.
chapters.depth: Explain NRZ, NRZI, Manchester, Differential Manchester, bipolar (AMI), and 4B/5B. Define terms unipolar, polar, and line code. Mention that line coding affects bandwidth and DC content.

figure.title: Line coding examples
figure.aria: Shows the voltage representation for NRZ and Manchester coding.

chapters.example: Encode the bit sequence 1101001 using Manchester coding and draw the waveform. What is the required bandwidth?
chapters.trap: Forgetting that Manchester doubles the minimum bandwidth compared to NRZ.
chapters.leave: Scrambling and error‑detecting line codes are covered later.

chapters.idea: Carry information by varying a carrier’s amplitude, frequency or phase.
chapters.depth: Describe analog modulation (AM, DSB‑SC, FM, PM) and digital modulation (ASK, FSK, PSK, QPSK). Define carrier, baseband, and bandwidth. Also known as shift keying for digital schemes.

figure.aria: Shows the flow from baseband data through a modulator, channel and demodulator.

chapters.example: Transmit 10 kbps using BPSK over a 1 MHz channel. Using the Shannon limit, find the minimum required SNR.
chapters.trap: Confusing carrier frequency with the channel bandwidth needed for the modulation.
chapters.leave: Higher‑order QAM and OFDM are discussed in advanced courses.

chapters.idea: Share a single physical link among many users or services.
chapters.depth: Explain Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM) with guard bands, Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) – synchronous and statistical, and Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM) for fibre. Also called frequency‑division, time‑division, and optical‑division multiplexing.

figure.aria: Illustrates how multiple signals are combined and later separated.

chapters.example: Three voice channels each 4 kHz are combined using FDM with a 0.5 kHz guard band. What total bandwidth is required?
chapters.trap: Forgetting to add guard bands between adjacent frequency slots.
chapters.leave: Statistical multiplexing algorithms are covered in networking electives.

chapters.idea: Spread a narrow‑band signal over a wide frequency range for security and interference resistance.
chapters.depth: Introduce Direct Sequence Spread Spectrum (DSSS) and Frequency Hopping Spread Spectrum (FHSS). Define chip rate, processing gain, and pseudo‑random code. Also called spreading codes.

figure.aria: Shows the steps of spreading a data stream and later despreading.

chapters.example: A 1 Mbps BPSK stream is spread with a 10 Mbps chip sequence. Compute the processing gain in dB.
chapters.trap: Assuming spreading reduces the net data rate instead of increasing robustness.
chapters.leave: CDMA system design is treated in advanced wireless courses.
